summary.text: The pharaoh was the monarch of ancient Egypt.
As king he owned all the land in Egypt, enacted laws, collected taxes and served as commander-in-chief of the military.
He also stood in for the deities as civil and religious administrator, and was responsible for maintaining Maat, or cosmic order, balance and justice.

facts.label: Original meaning
facts.value: The royal palace, not the person

facts.label: Earliest confirmed address
facts.value: A letter to Akhenaten, c. 1353–1336 BCE

facts.label: Combined crown
facts.value: The Pschent, red and white crowns together

facts.label: Rulers called pharaoh
facts.value: Scholars apply it from c. 3150 to 30 BCE

items.prompt: The word 'pharaoh' comes from a phrase meaning 'great house'. What did that phrase originally name?
items.explain: The phrase was the title of the royal palace, and only later became a way to address the ruler.

items.prompt: Egyptian kings were charged with keeping Maat. What did it stand for?

options.label: The army's loyalty to the throne

items.explain: Maat is cosmic order, balance and justice, and the king was responsible for maintaining it.

items.prompt: Before unification, Lower Egypt's kings wore the Red Crown and Upper Egypt's the White Crown. What became the pharaoh's official crown once the two kingdoms joined?

options.label: The Red Crown alone, from Lower Egypt
The White Crown alone, from Upper Egypt
The Khat, a headdress added later

items.explain: After unification the Pschent, a combination of the red and white crowns, became the official crown. Other headdresses came with later dynasties.

items.prompt: In ancient Egypt, who decided where new temples would be built?

options.label: A council of the leading priests
The king, in his religious role

items.explain: In his religious role, the king officiated at ceremonies and chose the sites of new temples.

items.prompt: Pharaoh was a word for the palace before it became a way to address the ruler. Which king received the earliest confirmed letter addressing him by it?
items.explain: The earliest confirmed instance is a letter to Akhenaten; Thutmose III is only a possibility that depends on an inscription.

items.prompt: Egyptians saw religion as central to everyday life. What part did the king play between the deities and the people?

options.label: Go-between for the deities and the people
Rival to the deities for the people's loyalty
Servant who took orders from temple priests
Observer who left worship to the scribes

items.explain: One of the king's roles was as an intermediary between the deities and the people.

paragraphs.heading: The king of Egypt
paragraphs.text: A pharaoh was the monarch of ancient Egypt. Scholars now use the title for every Egyptian ruler from the First Dynasty, around 3150 BCE, until the Roman Republic annexed Egypt in 30 BCE. The king acted as a go-between linking the gods and the people, and so stood in for the gods as both civil and religious administrator. He owned all the land, made laws, collected taxes and commanded the army. He also led religious ceremonies and picked the sites for new temples.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping order
paragraphs.text: Religion sat at the centre of everyday life in Egypt, and the pharaoh was the required link between gods and humans. For the gods, he made sure temple rituals were carried out properly. For the people, he guaranteed good harvests, defence of the land and fair justice. He was also responsible for Maat, an idea of cosmic order, balance and justice. Upholding Maat could mean going to war, either to defend Egypt or to attack others when that was believed to serve Maat, for example to gain resources.

paragraphs.heading: A word for a palace
paragraphs.text: The word pharaoh comes from the Egyptian phrase pr ꜥꜣ, meaning great house. It was written with two hieroglyphs, one meaning house and one meaning column, here used to mean great or high. At first the phrase named the royal palace and appeared only inside longer expressions, such as a title for a courtier of the palace. From the Twelfth Dynasty it also appeared in a wish that the Great House might live, prosper and be healthy, still meaning the building and not a person. Before the Eighteenth Dynasty, the term pointed to the king's administration more than to the king himself.

paragraphs.heading: From building to ruler
paragraphs.text: Sometime in the New Kingdom, people began to use pharaoh as a way to address the king. The earliest sure case is a letter to King Akhenaten of the Eighteenth Dynasty, who reigned around 1353 to 1336 BCE. An inscription at the Temple of Armant may show the title applied earlier, to Thutmose III, if it can be confirmed to refer to him. In the Eighteenth Dynasty the word became a respectful name for the ruler, and it was later applied back to all earlier kings.

paragraphs.heading: Part of the royal name
paragraphs.text: Around the late Twenty-first Dynasty, in the tenth century BCE, pharaoh began to be placed before the king's name along with his other titles. The first dated example comes from Year 17 of King Siamun, in the Karnak Priestly Annals, where a man's entry into the priesthood of Amun is dated to the reign of Pharaoh Siamun. His successor Psusennes II and the kings of the Twenty-second Dynasty kept up the habit. The Large Dakhla stela, for instance, is dated to Year 5 of Pharaoh Shoshenq, the founder of that dynasty. From the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, in ordinary use, it was the only title placed in front of the king's name.

paragraphs.heading: Crowns and names
paragraphs.text: Before Upper and Lower Egypt were united, the Red Crown, or Deshret, stood for the kingdom of Lower Egypt, while kings of Upper Egypt wore the White Crown, or Hedjet. After the two kingdoms joined, the Pschent, which combined the red and white crowns, became the pharaoh's official crown. Over time other headdresses came in, such as the Nemes, the Atef and the Khepresh. Early kings also had up to three formal titles, including the Horus name, and two more, the Golden Horus and the nomen, were added later.

paragraphs.heading: The word travels
paragraphs.text: In Late Egyptian it is reconstructed as sounding like parʕoʔ, and from it came the Hebrew form in the Bible, then Greek pharaō and Late Latin pharaō. The Qur'an spells it firʿawn in Arabic, keeping the Egyptian ayin sound and taking the -n ending from Greek. English first wrote Pharao, until the translators of the King James Bible brought back the final h from Hebrew.
